system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), classic Richardson syndrome phenotype
mechanism: Progressive supranuclear palsy is an atypical parkinsonian neurodegenerative tauopathy. Pathology includes predominantly 4-repeat tau accumulation in neurons and glia with degeneration involving basal ganglia and brainstem/oculomotor structures. The classic clinical phenotype combines early postural instability with backward falls, axial-predominant rigidity, and supranuclear impairment of vertical eye movements.
vignette: A 68-year-old man is evaluated for 2 years of progressive gait difficulty and slowed movement. During the first year of illness, he began falling unexpectedly, usually backward. A trial of carbidopa/levodopa produced little improvement. Examination shows bradykinesia and marked rigidity of the neck and trunk with a relatively extended posture. Resting tremor is minimal. When he follows the examiner's finger, vertical saccades are markedly slowed and downward gaze is limited; horizontal eye movements are much less affected.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractor_notes: Idiopathic Parkinson disease can cause bradykinesia and rigidity, but early backward falls, axial-predominant extended posture, prominent vertical gaze impairment, and little levodopa benefit favor progressive supranuclear palsy. Parkinson disease more often has a flexed posture and a stronger levodopa response.

Multiple system atrophy is another atypical parkinsonian disorder and may respond poorly to levodopa, but prominent autonomic dysfunction and/or cerebellar features are characteristic. Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy with early backward falls and axial rigidity is more characteristic of progressive supranuclear palsy.

Corticobasal syndrome can cause parkinsonism, but it classically has an asymmetric limb-predominant presentation with cortical features such as apraxia, cortical sensory loss, myoclonus, dystonia, or an alien-limb phenomenon. The symmetric axial pattern with vertical gaze impairment favors progressive supranuclear palsy.

Dementia with Lewy bodies can produce parkinsonism, but early cognitive decline with fluctuations, recurrent visual hallucinations, and REM sleep behavior disorder are characteristic clues. The dominant pattern here is early postural instability plus axial rigidity and vertical supranuclear gaze dysfunction.
key_expl: This patient has progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP). The most discriminating combination is early unexplained backward falls, axial-predominant rigidity with an extended posture, minimal response to levodopa, and marked slowing/limitation of vertical eye movements, especially downward gaze. PSP is an atypical parkinsonian syndrome associated with tau pathology and is explicitly included in the 2026 USMLE Nervous System content outline.
objective: Recognize progressive supranuclear palsy in an older adult with early backward falls, axial rigidity, poor levodopa response, and vertical supranuclear gaze impairment.
clues: falls beginning during the first year of illness
markedly slowed vertical saccades with impaired downgaze
